indicators.note: upset means the letters of the two words late and damp are knocked over and rearranged

explanation.surface: A gardener complains that a wet, late season has spoiled the harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' tells you to rearrange the eight letters of LATE DAMP.
explanation.definitionFit: This tree bears the sweet brown fruit of desert oases, so it is literally a grower of fruit.

parts.note: to debar someone is to keep them out or exclude them
K is the chess and card abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A ruler is refused entry to a country.
explanation.definitionFit: To disembark from a ship is to land, an old verb for going ashore.

clue.text: Not a single woman will be seen wearing this

definitions.text: Not a single woman will be seen wearing this

parts.words: Not a single woman will be seen wearing this
parts.note: the outfit and linen gathered by a bride for her marriage: once married she is no longer single

explanation.surface: A fashion warning that no lone woman would be caught in some garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not a single woman' reads as 'no woman at all', but it means a woman who is no longer single: a bride.
explanation.definitionFit: A bride's collection of clothes for married life is worn by someone who has just stopped being single.

clue.text: Spend a lot of time in sea journey

parts.note: to pass time is to spend it
an age is a very long period of time

explanation.surface: Someone passes many hours on a long ocean voyage.
explanation.definitionFit: A voyage by ship, especially a booked crossing, is called a sea passage.

explanation.surface: A statement that an unconstrained thing is bound to be imprecise.
explanation.definitionFit: Something untied is free, not bound; a free translation or vague estimate is likewise imprecise.

clue.text: Maxim, for example, to follow as pointer, perhaps

parts.note: the Maxim was an early machine gun, named after its inventor Hiram Maxim
to dog someone is to follow them closely

explanation.surface: A saying offered as guidance, with instructions to follow it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maxim' looks like a saying, but it is the Maxim machine gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A pointer is a breed of hunting dog that indicates game, one example of a shooting dog.

parts.note: under means less than, as in under ten
a go can mean a success, as in making a go of it

explanation.surface: Life lessons in falling short of achievement.
explanation.definitionFit: To go through something, such as surgery or a test, is to experience it.

clue.text: Flood from river in part of Ireland

indicators.note: in places the river's letter inside the name of the Irish county

parts.note: Down is a county of Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: A river bursts its banks in an Irish district.
explanation.walkthrough: County Down is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: To flood something is to submerge it entirely, as fields under water.

clue.text: Gallery aims to provide unexpected pleasures

parts.note: the gods is the highest gallery in a theatre
ends are aims or goals, as in ends and means

explanation.surface: An art gallery sets out to delight its visitors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gallery' suggests art, but the gods is the cheap top balcony of a British theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: Windfalls arriving as if sent from heaven are welcome surprises.

indicators.note: involved suggests the letters of aspirant are tangled up into a new order

explanation.surface: A hopeful politician gets mixed up with a single political party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' signals the rearrangement of ASPIRANT; 'with one party' is the definition, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A biased supporter sides firmly with one faction or cause.

clue.text: Vacillates between heavy strokes and taps?

parts.note: blows are heavy strikes or punches
a basin's pair of taps are marked H and C for the two water temperatures

explanation.surface: Someone wavers between hard hits and gentle tapping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taps' looks like light blows to pair with heavy strokes, but it means the two water taps of a sink.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone who keeps changing their mind, now keen, now indifferent.

parts.note: a rose is a flower, and Rose is a girl's name
to dine is to eat, so dined means ate

explanation.surface: A cheerful flower seller has had her dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose-coloured, a pinkish tint, figuratively means hopeful, as in seeing through rose-tinted spectacles.

explanation.surface: A classical dramatist was succeeded by a twentieth-century one.
explanation.walkthrough: Terentius was the Roman comic playwright; Rattigan was the English playwright whose first name came before his surname, so Rattigan follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman comic dramatist shares his English name with the first name that precedes Rattigan.

clue.text: Greek hero held back by unusual enemy

indicators.note: held back says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A Greek warrior is restrained by a strange foe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held back' means read backwards: the letters run back through unUSUAL ENEMy.
explanation.definitionFit: The king of Sparta, husband of Helen, led forces in the Trojan War of Greek legend.

parts.note: laundry that has been aired has been dried off fully
stout is a dark beer, a kind of ale

explanation.surface: A fat dog has been dried off after a bath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stout' looks like an adjective describing the dog, but it is the beer.
explanation.definitionFit: This large terrier breed comes from a valley in Yorkshire.

clue.text: Tight as a piston should be?

explanation.surface: Mechanical advice on how snugly a piston should fit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tight' is slang for drunk; a well-maintained piston is lubricated.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for drunk, and also lubricated, the state of a smoothly running engine part.

parts.note: Freemasons meet in lodges, so they are lodge members, lodgemen

indicators.note: end of the word west means its final letter alone

explanation.surface: Freemasons place money in a bank in London's West End.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West End' looks like London's theatre district, but it means the last letter of West.
explanation.definitionFit: A deposit, such as a layer of sediment, is something lodged in place.

parts.note: a pawn shop read as a shop selling only pawns would lack most of the board pieces: kings, queens, rooks and the rest

explanation.surface: A complaint that most items can't be found at the pawnbroker's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pawn-shop' reads as a pawnbroker, but think of a shop that stocks only the humblest chess piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The figures used in the board game, of which only the pawns would be sold in a shop of pawns.

indicators.note: conclusion of signals taking the final letter of English

parts.note: an aunt is a relative

explanation.surface: An English relative regularly comes to the end of things.
explanation.definitionFit: To frequent a place is to visit it habitually, as ghosts do their old homes.

clue.text: Labour finding odd. Tory constituents an advantage

indicators.note: odd picks the letters in odd positions of the word Tory
constituents are the parts making up the word Tory, of which the odd ones are taken

parts.note: avail means benefit or advantage, as in to no avail

explanation.surface: A Labour politician sees an advantage in strange voters in a Tory seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' looks like the British political party, but it is hard work.
explanation.definitionFit: Toil, hard and painful work, is what this old word for effort means.

indicators.note: holds means the author's name contains the other piece

parts.note: Charles Reade was a Victorian novelist, author of The Cloister and the Hearth

indicators.note: back means the word for information is turned round

parts.note: gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: A rebellious writer withholds facts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' makes NEG from GEN; 'holds' puts that inside READE.
explanation.definitionFit: A turncoat or deserter is someone who rebels against a cause.

clue.text: Gee, girls, you'll be ignored by passing men in these

definitions.text: you'll be ignored by passing men in these

parts.note: gee is the spelt-out name of the letter G
lasses are girls

explanation.surface: Girls are warned that men will pass them by if they wear spectacles.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition echoes Dorothy Parker: 'Men seldom make passes at girls who wear glasses'.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectacles, the eyewear that the old quip says keeps flirting men away.

parts.note: in a down entry, one word written upward spells pets

explanation.surface: A bare instruction: get more animals.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: the answer, read as an instruction for a down clue, writes a four-letter word upward to make 'pets'.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise the rate or intensity of something is to boost it.

clue.text: Directed towards main South- East prize

parts.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south
E is the compass abbreviation for east
an award is a prize

explanation.surface: A trophy is presented in the south-east of the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'main' is the old poetic word for the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Heading toward the ocean, the main being a poetic name for the open sea.

clue.text: Joint leaders of Alliance naturally knock Labour effort

indicators.note: leaders of tells you to take the first letter of each following word

explanation.surface: Joint heads of a political alliance criticise Labour's campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' looks like an adjective with 'leaders', but it is the definition: a body joint.
explanation.definitionFit: The joint connecting foot to leg.

parts.note: a bra is an item of women's underwear
a vest is a British undershirt

explanation.surface: Asks who deserves the loveliest lingerie.
explanation.walkthrough: Dryden wrote 'None but the brave deserves the fair', so the most courageous deserve the fairest. A vest in Britain is an undershirt.
explanation.definitionFit: Proverbially only courageous people win beauty, so the most courageous earn the loveliest.

explanation.surface: A call to oppose a party at the ballot box.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the first definition as a slogan: 'Be a no!', an exhortation to vote no. The second is British slang for a lively party.
explanation.definitionFit: A campaign slogan telling voters to say no, and an old British word for a festive knees-up.

clue.text: Did Grimes in Bath succeed so completely?

definitions.text: Did Grimes in Bath succeed so completely?

parts.words: Did Grimes in Bath succeed so completely?
parts.note: Grimes is the chimney-sweep master in The Water-Babies; a sweep bathing would scrub himself thoroughly clean, an idiom for total victory

explanation.surface: Wonders whether a man named Grimes triumphed totally in the city of Bath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bath' looks like the English city, but it is a tub: Grimes, the sweep in Kingsley's The Water-Babies, washing himself.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means winning everything or getting rid of everything, as a broom clears a floor.

explanation.surface: A compass part is essential for someone doing needlework.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sewer' is one who sews, not a drain.
explanation.definitionFit: The magnetised pointer of a compass, and the sharp tool every seamstress threads.

clue.text: Musical position of fiddler may get a slating

explanation.surface: A musician's place in the band is criticised.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical is Fiddler on the Roof; roofs are covered with slates, and 'a slating' also means harsh criticism.
explanation.definitionFit: The top of a building, where the musical's violinist perches, and which a roofer covers with slates.
